Running command: clear; cat > /tmp/a2.py <<'EOF'
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
tier = pd.CategoricalDtype(["gold", "silver", "bronze"], ordered=True)
idx = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([["bronze", "gold", "silver"], [1, 2]], names=["tier", "quarter"])
report = pd.DataFrame({"revenue": [10, 11, 20, 21, 30, 31]}, index=idx)
report.index = report.index.set_levels(report.index.levels[0].astype(tier), level="tier")
mi = report.index
print(mi.levels[0], mi.codes)
print("level monotonic:", [l.is_monotonic_increasing for l in mi.levels])
print("lexsorted:", mi._is_lexsorted(), mi._lexsort_depth)
vals=[mi._get_level_values(i)._values for i in reversed(range(2))]
print(type(vals[1]), np.asarray(vals[1]), np.lexsort(vals))
print("slm is self:", mi._sort_levels_monotonic() is mi)
print("dec:", mi.is_monotonic_decreasing)
# variants
r2 = report.iloc[[2,3,0,1,4,5]]
print("gold-first:", r2.index.codes[0].tolist(), r2.index.is_monotonic_increasing, r2.sort_index().index.get_level_values(0).tolist())
r3 = report.iloc[::-1]
print("reversed:", r3.index.is_monotonic_increasing, r3.sort_index().index.get_level_values(0).tolist())
df = report.reset_index(); df["tier"]=df["tier"].astype(tier)
r4 = df.set_index(["tier","quarter"])
print("set_index levels:", r4.index.levels[0].tolist(), r4.index.codes[0].tolist(), r4.sort_index().index.get_level_values(0).tolist())
un = pd.CategoricalDtype(["gold", "silver", "bronze"], ordered=False)
r5 = report.copy(); r5.index = idx.set_levels(idx.levels[0].astype(un), level="tier")
print("unordered:", r5.index.is_monotonic_increasing, r5.sort_index().index.get_level_values(0).tolist())
ci = pd.CategoricalIndex(["bronze","gold","silver"], dtype=tier)
print("1-level:", ci.is_monotonic_increasing, ci.sort_values().tolist())
print("sort_values:", df.sort_values(["tier","quarter"]).tier.tolist())
EOF

I'm checking how masked NaN values get treated: with uses_mask they count as non-NA, so the max stays at -inf and the count still goes up, which gives -inf for that group. Now I'm looking for where in group_min_max the mask decides whether an entry is NA.

I'm checking whether the four reproductions share one cause, and the upstream `group_min_max` code suggests one: when `uses_mask` is set, NaN values are never examined, only the mask is, so they get ignored instead of being treated as NA. Sum propagates NaN, and first returns it, so the gap shows up only in min/max.

I'm tracing the MultiIndex monotonicity check: the first level is a categorical with a custom category order, and the check falls through to a lexsort that converts it to strings, so the order comes out alphabetical rather than by category.

I'm working out how the MultiIndex check goes wrong: the codes are already lexsorted, so it treats the index as monotonic and never reorders the levels. That holds even though the level order bronze, gold, silver isn't monotonic, so sorting by level just leaves the codes as they are. The descending case is next.

I'm checking whether the descending case hits the same problem: the reversed index isn't monotonic, so it falls through to sorting on the codes, which were never remapped to the sorted level order. That gives silver, gold, bronze instead of the right order. Next I want to see whether a different starting row order changes the result.

Next I'm checking the MultiIndex case with the rows in other orders: if the codes aren't lexsorted, the early return is skipped and the levels get remapped, so the result comes out right. The reversed-rows variant is skipped the same way. Then I'm looking at how `set_index` builds the levels from a categorical column, since it keeps the category order.

I'm tracing the cause in `MultiIndex.is_monotonic_increasing`: for a categorical level it falls back to `np.lexsort` on the object-converted values, so it compares alphabetically and wrongly reports the index as monotonic. That flag then makes `_sort_levels_monotonic` return early, so the levels never get remapped to the sorted order.

I'm checking what upstream `MultiIndex.is_monotonic_increasing` does: if every level is monotonic it trusts the codes, otherwise it falls back to `np.lexsort` over the level values.

I'm checking the sort-order fallback in the MultiIndex monotonicity code: for non-monotonic categorical levels it runs `np.lexsort` over the string-converted values, so the category order is ignored and the index is wrongly reported as monotonic.

I'm thinking about whether to use the per-level codes mapped through each level's rank instead of the object-converted values, since that would respect the categorical order. One option is to take each extension array's `_values_for_argsort()` so a Categorical contributes its codes, or to remap codes via each level's argsort.

I'm checking whether the upstream fallback in `is_monotonic_increasing` could use each level's `_values_for_argsort()` for extension arrays, so a categorical contributes its codes and respects the category order. Since lexsort is stable, that should keep the nonunique case correct, and I still need to confirm that the other callers, like `is_monotonic_decreasing` and `_sort_levels_monotonic`, rely on that same check.

I'm considering which routines call `MultiIndex.is_monotonic_increasing` in the sort path, since a wrong answer there would skip the level remapping. Next I'm checking the analogous case for a plain index, where `stack` factorizes the index and NaN gets its own code and level.

Next I'm checking the other side of the problem: for a plain index, `stack` factorizes with NaN kept as its own code, so NaN ends up inside the levels instead of being coded -1. Then a lookup for NaN goes through the -1 path and misses the matching entry.

I'm now checking the NaN side of the same picture: in `stack`, a plain index gets factorized with NaN kept as its own code, so NaN lands inside the levels rather than being coded -1. Lookups for NaN then take the -1 path and miss the entry. I'm also looking at the column-level variant, where the dropped level is a plain Index rather than a MultiIndex.

I'm checking where `stack_v3` builds the column levels from a plain index: `factorize` keeps NaN as its own code instead of `-1`, so the bug repeats at a second spot inside the function. I'll look through `reshape` for other places that build a MultiIndex this way with `verify_integrity=False`.

I'm checking why the stack code uses `use_na_sentinel=False`: as written, NaN gets its own level instead of the -1 code that a MultiIndex expects. Using the default sentinel would map NaN to -1, which matches how levels are meant to be built. I recall upstream stack_v3 doing exactly this in both the index and column branches, so this looks like a real upstream bug rather than something specific to this repro.

I'm working out the fix for `stack_v3`: the `factorize` calls with `use_na_sentinel=False` put NaN inside the levels instead of coding it -1. Switching to the default sentinel and building the column levels from `factorize` output would keep NaN out of the levels. I still need to check how `MultiIndex.get_loc` handles the -1 code.

Now I'm checking how `MultiIndex.isin` and the `get_loc` path handle a NaN that sits inside the levels, since that's where the stack bug would show up. Separately, I'm looking at the masked `group_min_max` case: a NaN with mask False is neither greater nor less than the starting values, so it never updates the result, yet it still counts as an observation. That would make the group come out as -inf, or as 2.0 for `[nan, 2.0]`, rather than propagating NaN, and I need to decide whether NaN-propagation is the expected behavior here.

I'm weighing whether the masked NaN should propagate as NaN, the way an ungrouped max or a sum would, instead of being silently skipped and leaving -inf behind. The cumulative variant in `group_cummin_max` handles the masked case the same way, so I'll check that next.

I'm checking which other inline spots handle masked NaN the same way: group_sum, group_prod, and other reductions with an `if uses_mask` branch. The `mask[i, j]` check, together with the `_treat_as_na` fallback, may repeat across many of them.

I'm going through the other masked reductions that branch on `uses_mask`, since arithmetic like sum or mean already propagates NaN, while first and last only depend on the mask and look correct. The real trouble is in the comparison-based routines: a masked NaN that isn't marked missing gets compared against the ±inf starting values, never wins either test, and leaves the result at -inf.

I'm thinking about the masked path in `group_min_max`: a NaN that isn't flagged as missing still gets counted as an observation, but the `>`/`<` comparisons never accept it, so the result stays at the ±inf starting value. I'd need to propagate NaN in that branch for float types rather than silently dropping it.

I'm considering the comparison in the masked path: a NaN that isn't flagged as missing never wins `>` or `<`, so it never overwrites the starting value. Adding an `or val != val` check would let that NaN propagate into the result, and I'd still need to apply the same change to the cumulative variant.

Now I'm checking whether masked.py's `_groupby_op` has any handling for NaN under the distinguish option, by searching for uses of `distinguish_nan_and_na`. Separately, I'm looking at the `_set_item` path for a 1-D extension array like Int64: the tiling step is skipped, so the value goes straight into `_set_item_mgr` and through `iset` as an extension value.

I'm checking how `_sanitize_column` handles a Series, since the 1-D extension array path seems to avoid tiling only for Series values.

Checking whether `__setitem__` handles a duplicated column differently before `_set_item` runs, since the tiling step only gets skipped in one path.

I'm now checking the datetime-column case: a partial-string key like "2024" resolves to a slice of two columns, so the 1-D numpy value isn't tiled, and the block shape check fails with "Got 2 positions but value has 1 columns." For an Int64 column the same path shares one array across both blocks, so the two columns end up tied.

I'm tracing the root cause as a shared-memory problem: for a one-dimensional extension array with several target positions, the block manager reuses the same array object for each placement without copying, so the blocks end up tied together. I'm also looking at whether the skipped broadcast in `_set_item` is the decision that sends it down that path.

I'm now checking the `iset` path for extension values: `value_getitem` hands back the same array for every placement, so each new block wraps that one object. I think that's the decision where the columns end up sharing memory, so I'll look at the `MultiIndex` and categorical cases next to see whether they follow the same route.

I'm wondering whether a plain integer-location `iset` shares memory the same way, since each `inv["a"] = arr` copies the array through `_sanitize_column`, but within one statement a single copy may end up backing several blocks. The Series case seems to avoid that, so I need to test which path `__setitem__` takes for it.

I'm settling on where the shared-memory bug starts: in `BlockManager.iset`, an extension value gets reused as-is for every placement, so each new block wraps the same array object. A copy for each block beyond the first would break that tie, and I'm weighing that against fixing the broadcast decision earlier in `DataFrame._set_item`.

I'm checking whether `inplace=True` is ever passed into `_iset_item_mgr` or `iset`, since that path would reuse the same extension value object across existing blocks too.

I'm looking at why the inplace path might also share one array across blocks: `iset` reuses the extension value object for every new block, so the same reuse could happen there too. I'll confirm which callers pass `inplace=True` before deciding whether the fix belongs in `iset` or in `_set_item`.

Next I'll test the four suspected causes directly, starting with the MultiIndex monotonic check.
